text: You're in one of the greatest food cities on earth that happens to also have a giant orange bridge. Tell me — are you here to eat, explore, party, or all of the above? I've got opinions on all of it.

Now we're talking. What's the vibe? If you want the tasting menu experience, Wolfsbane in Dogpatch is the most exciting thing in SF right now. For something more chill but equally serious, Side A on 16th Street has a vinyl collection, a killer burger, and Parisian gnocchi that haunts your dreams. On a budget? La Taqueria on Mission — no rice, just the perfect burrito.

SF's modern Chinese wave is real. Happy Crane on Gough has the Peking duck and dim sum nailed. Mister Jiu's in Chinatown is the OG — order the banquet. For Japanese, Rintaro is where every chef in the city eats after service. And if you just need a bowl of ramen, Marufuku in Japantown is the call.

Swan Oyster Depot on Polk — 18 seats, no reservations, cash only, open since 1912. Get there by 10:30 or plan to wait. If that's too intense, Hog Island at the Ferry Building has perfect oysters with a bay view. Tuesday happy hour there is the local move. During crab season (Nov-June), get a whole cracked Dungeness at Fisherman's Wharf — the sidewalk stands are legit.

For tasting menus, Wolfsbane is the hottest seat in town right now. Mijoté in the Mission is a James Beard nominee — $84 for four courses of French-Japanese perfection. Enclos out in Sonoma has two Michelin stars inside year one. And Bourbon Steak at the Westin St. Francis does tableside wagyu tomahawk if you want theatrics.

Smuggler's Cove — three floors of tiki perfection, 400+ rums, one of the best bars in the world. Period. For speakeasy vibes, The Felix has a hidden entrance through a picture frame. The Tonga Room at the Fairmont has an indoor lagoon and actual rainstorms. And if you want a proper dive, Zeitgeist's beer garden is the most San Francisco thing that exists.

Do this: Alcatraz in the morning (book 90 days ahead!), then walk the Golden Gate in the afternoon. The next day, take the Powell-Hyde cable car to Lombard Street, walk down to Fisherman's Wharf, then cab to the Mission for tacos and Dolores Park. That's the greatest hits. After that, get off the beaten path — Filbert Steps, the Presidio, Ocean Beach at sunset.

Rent a bike at Blazing Saddles, ride across the Golden Gate to Sausalito, ferry back. Classic SF day. The Presidio has trails with bridge views and zero tourists. Golden Gate Park has a bison paddock, Japanese Tea Garden, and paddleboats. Crissy Field is the flat waterfront walk. Ocean Beach has surf but the water is freezing and the currents are serious.

Ferry Building Saturday market for artisan food finds. City Lights Bookstore in North Beach for the best bookstore in America. Valencia Street in the Mission for vintage, design shops, and indie boutiques. Skip the Wharf tourist shops — you don't need a Alcatraz snow globe.

Blue Bottle started here — the Mint Plaza flagship is still great for a pour-over. Philz in the Mission does the Mint Mojito Iced Coffee that'll change your life. For the vinyl-listener energy, Kissaten Hifi plays 1950s jazz while you sip. Tartine's morning bun with a coffee is a spiritual experience.

Hotel Drisco in Pacific Heights is quietly the best hotel in the city — included breakfast, wine reception, neighborhood feel. The Fairmont on Nob Hill is grand-dame luxury with the Tonga Room in the basement. For budget with personality, Phoenix Hotel is a rock-and-roll motor lodge with a pool. The Lodge at the Presidio is charming if you want to walk to the bridge.

BART from SFO airport to downtown is $9.65 and takes 30 min. Don't rent a car unless you're leaving the city — parking is $40-60/day and the hills will stress you out. MUNI buses cover everything. Cable cars are $8/ride or get the $24 day pass. Uber/Lyft work great. For the bridge ride, rent a bike.

California Academy of Sciences is the slam dunk — aquarium, planetarium, and rainforest under one roof. The Exploratorium on Pier 15 is hands-on science that adults love too. Ride the cable car, see the sea lions at Pier 39, then head to Golden Gate Park for the playground and paddleboats. Oracle Park for a Giants game is great for kids.

Mijoté for a candlelit French-Japanese dinner in the Mission. Walk the Golden Gate at sunset from Crissy Field. Cocktails at Smuggler's Cove, then late-night at The Felix. For a big splurge, Wolfsbane's tasting menu with wine pairings. The Lodge at the Presidio for a quiet, romantic stay.

Perfect SF day: 8am Ferry Building Saturday market. 10am cable car to Lombard Street. 11am walk through North Beach — espresso at Caffe Trieste, browse City Lights. Noon lunch at Rintaro. 2pm bike across the Golden Gate to Sausalito, ferry back. 5pm Dolores Park sunset. 7pm dinner at Side A. 9pm Smuggler's Cove for a nightcap. You're welcome.

Check sf.funcheap.com — it's the local bible for free and cheap events. Stern Grove has free Sunday concerts all summer. NightLife Thursdays at the Academy of Sciences. After Dark Thursdays at the Exploratorium. And if you're here in October, Hardly Strictly Bluegrass is a free 3-day festival in Golden Gate Park that's pure magic.

Tartine morning bun. That's the answer. But also: the Saturday Ferry Building market for grazing. Plow on Potrero Hill for the lemon ricotta pancakes. And if you want dim sum for breakfast (you should), head to Chinatown before 10am when it's locals only.

SF is not a late-night city — let's be honest. But: Zeitgeist's beer garden stays open. The Saloon in North Beach has live blues until 2am. Emporium Arcade Bar is packed until close. For late-night food, the taco trucks on Harrison in the Mission run past midnight.

Napa is 90 min north. Sonoma is more chill and often better value. But if you don't want to leave the city, Big Finish Wine Tavern in the Mission has affordable glasses. Key Klub on Bush Street is the natural wine spot. And the Ferry Building has tastings on Saturdays. For a proper day trip, book through one of the shuttle services from Fisherman's Wharf.

Layers. Always layers. The sun might be blazing in the Mission while it's 55°F and foggy at the bridge — that's a 15-degree swing in 3 miles. Bring a windbreaker. September-October is the real summer (locals call it Indian Summer). June-July are actually the foggiest months. Yes, we named the fog Karl.
